body: The spec is admirably concrete about pipelines and statistics, but it quietly sidesteps the epistemological heart of the project: there is no ground truth anywhere. Both Pylint and the LLM are detectors, not oracles, so 'detection rates' measured by McNemar's test tell us only that the two tools disagree at some rate — not which one is right, or whether the LLM's 'Long Method' call is a true positive or a fluent hallucination. The spec's own assumption concedes this ('a "rule-based reference" rather than an absolute ground truth'), yet User Story 3 still promises to report 'the set of smells detected *only* by static analysis and *only* by the LLM' as if these were validated findings rather than unadjudicated claims. Complementarity cannot be established by union/intersection alone; it needs at least a manually labeled gold subset. Second, the taxonomy-matching problem is asserted away: Pylint emits codes like C0111 (missing docstring — a style issue, not a smell) while the LLM is prompted to produce free-text smell names; the spec assumes these label spaces are comparable ('semantically comparable enough') but specifies no mapping or normalization procedure, without which the overlap analysis in FR-006 and the per-category comparison is undefined. Third, there is a tautology risk the spec names but does not resolve: predicting static-only detection from cyclomatic complexity when Pylint's own rules (R0912, R0915) threshold on complexity is circular — the logistic regression would largely rediscover Pylint's rulebook. A held-out human-labeled sample (even 100 functions) and an explicit label-alignment table would convert this from an engineering plan into a study that can actually answer its research question. Minor: the feature branch name '001-gene-regulation' appears to be a copy-paste remnant from an unrelated project.
